subject: Economics
central_question: How can one statistical index summarise relative change across a group of related prices, quantities, or other economic variables?
in_scope_units: Introduction to the need for a single summary measure of change in a group of related variables.
Meaning of an index number, base period, current period, price index, and quantity index.
Construction of simple and weighted price indexes through aggregative methods.
Laspeyres and Paasche weighted aggregative price indexes and the role of base-period and current-period quantities.
Simple and weighted methods of averaging price relatives.
Consumer Price Index, Wholesale Price Index, Index of Industrial Production, Human Development Index, and Sensex.
Issues in constructing an index number, including purpose, item selection, base year, formula, weights, and data reliability.
Economic uses of CPI, WPI, IIP, agricultural production index, Sensex, purchasing power, and real wages.
Conclusion and recap on careful interpretation and policy use of index numbers.
banned_topics: Scatter diagrams and coefficients of correlation

known_pitfalls.claim: An index number of 250 means a rise of 250 percent from the base.
known_pitfalls.correction: With a base of 100, an index of 250 means the level is two and a half times the base, which is 150 percent above the base.

known_pitfalls.claim: Every item in a simple index receives importance according to expenditure share.
known_pitfalls.correction: A simple unweighted index treats items as equally important; a weighted index reflects relative importance.

known_pitfalls.claim: Laspeyres and Paasche indexes use the same quantity weights.
known_pitfalls.correction: Laspeyres uses base-period quantities, while Paasche uses current-period quantities.

known_pitfalls.claim: CPI and WPI measure the same price concept for the same users.
known_pitfalls.correction: CPI measures average change in retail prices for a consumer category, while WPI measures changes in wholesale goods prices and has no reference consumer category.

known_pitfalls.claim: Any convenient year is suitable as a base year.
known_pitfalls.correction: The base year should be normal, reasonably recent, and free from extreme or abnormal values.

recommended_example_progression: Use Cases 1–3 from the Introduction to motivate cost-of-living, Sensex, and inflation indexes.
Use NCERT Example 1 to introduce a simple aggregative price index and its limitations.
Use NCERT Example 2 to contrast Laspeyres and Paasche quantity weights.
Use NCERT Example 3 and Example 4 to compare weighted price relatives and CPI construction.
Use NCERT Exercise 21 to discuss why index series with different bases and consumer groups are not directly comparable.
ncert_end_of_chapter_exercises_reference: The embedded source chapter ends with EXERCISES 1–22 and activities on widely used indexes and purchasing power.
